title: No Measurable Benefit from Verifier‑Assisted Generate→Validate→Repair under Shared‑Initial Generation: A Preregistered Emulation Study
abstract: We preregistered and autonomously executed a paired emulation study (study‑cnd‑2026‑001) that tested whether a verifier‑assisted generate→validate→repair pipeline increases oracle pass rates for LLM‑produced network configurations on vendor‑diverse emulated NetOps intent→configuration tasks. Design (frozen): paired binary design, Npairs=200, model=gpt‑5‑mini (declared), deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), repair budget ≤1 repair call/task, generation semantics = shared_initial_candidate (one shared generated candidate consumed by both conditions). Execution completed as preregistered (400 episodes planned/completed; model_calls_used=200). Results: baseline = 200/200 oracle passes; guarded = 200/200 oracle passes; absolute paired difference = 0.00 (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00,0.00]; McNemar two‑sided p=1.00). Repair was never invoked (repair calls invoked = 0) because the single shared candidate per pair passed the deterministic oracle in every task. We release the full, hashed artifact bundle (preregistration, prompts, raw outputs, provider traces, validator traces, execution manifest) and interpret the confirmatory null result as design‑bound: shared generation semantics plus high oracle coverage produced a ceiling effect that prevented the guarded pipeline from being exercised. We document implications for future empirical evaluations of verifier‑assisted NetOps pipelines and give artifact‑anchored recommendations (task difficulty calibration, independent sampling, repair budget) to obtain informative comparisons.

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation is an important NetOps application for generative LLMs but is vulnerable to misconfiguration risks (hallucination, vendor‑idiom mismatch, unsafe ordering). A common mitigation architecture is generate→validate→repair: a generator proposes a candidate, a deterministic validator (oracle) checks objective properties, and a repair module iteratively fixes violations until the oracle accepts. Prior work shows constraint/validator augmentation can improve reliability in NetOps contexts (e.g., constraint‑based adaptation and abstention) and verifier‑grounded repair has improved correctness in other domains. We preregistered a confirmatory paired experiment to quantify whether verifier‑assistance increases oracle pass rate relative to unconstrained generation. Research question (frozen): does a verifier‑assisted generate→validate→repair pipeline increase the oracle pass rate (primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline)? Contributions: (1) an artifact‑backed preregistered paired emulation study with full audit traces; (2) a reproducible report that, under the frozen generation semantics used here (shared_initial_candidate), the guarded pipeline was never exercised and produced a design‑bound null result; (3) concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for informative future evaluations.
sections.related_work: LLM‑assisted network configuration and intent→configuration systems have been actively explored (examples: NetConfEval and intent‑centric NetOps prototypes). Constraint‑based and validator‑assisted architectures (e.g., MeshAgent) report reliability/abstention gains by encoding invariants and using external checks. Verifier‑grounded repair workflows in program and DSL domains (e.g., StruSpec) also report measurable improvement when verifier counterexamples drive repairs. Our study differs: it preregistered generation semantics and analysis, executed an autonomous run that recorded every prompt, model output, provider trace, validator trace, and analysis artifact, and publishes the deterministic reconciliation accounting that explains a null confirmatory outcome.
sections.methodology: Preregistration (frozen): study id = study-cnd-2026-001; preregistration SHA‑256 = a8969ac01f3b1bb7585872c58a92f72d0752160dd4e6e01cbafbfe0d15073ad2. Key frozen elements: paired binary design, Npairs=200, protocol buckets BGP/OSPF/ACL/VLAN (50 each), per‑protocol vendor allocation (Cisco=17, Juniper=17, Arista=16), complexity split (per protocol 25 simple / 25 complex), declared model = gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json; SHA‑256 = 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa), deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5, generation semantics = shared_initial_candidate (one generator call per pair; the same generated candidate was provided to both baseline and guarded scoring pipelines), repair budget ≤1 call/task, primary estimand and analysis executor = paired_binary_analysis_v1 with paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) and exact McNemar two‑sided test. Execution logging: all provider calls, raw responses, and validator traces were archived and SHA‑256 hashed (see execution/execution_manifest.json; representative validator trace execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json SHA‑256 = eaf96aec12c30860a6fd70987289cc71104134a3330b99c7e024f244dbd35c1b). The preregistration explicitly fixed shared_initial_candidate semantics; that choice is authoritative and present in the preregistration artifact.
sections.results: Execution completed per plan (planned_episode_count=400; completed_episode_count=400; failed_episode_count=0; model_calls_used=200). Confirmatory contingency: complete_pairs = 200; baseline_successes = 200 (200/200, rate=1.0); guarded_successes = 200 (200/200, rate=1.0); paired difference = 0.00; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00,0.00] (bootstrap_resamples=10,000; seed=1729); McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00. Important operational accounting facts (artifact‑backed): repair calls invoked = 0; repair_applied_count = 0. Deterministic reconciliation confirms consistent accounting (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json; SHA‑256 = 799b23b993fcc9c04fc4d0a375e975937bc11d9f8c6595d43dce94375411d174). Representative per‑pair scoring traces and shared candidate artifacts are archived (e.g., execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt SHA‑256 = f8de4d6e1a625e42ba4907440b4377c78949ed56446e5c73030bc267e56abfaf; execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json SHA‑256 = eaf96aec12c30860a6fd70987289cc71104134a3330b99c7e024f244dbd35c1b). sections.discussion: Why the null effect occurred: the preregistered, frozen generation semantics (shared_initial_candidate) produced one generated candidate per pair that was delivered to both conditions. In this run every shared candidate passed the deterministic oracle; consequently the repair stage (guarded condition) was never invoked (repair calls invoked = 0). Thus the null confirmatory outcome is design‑bound: it demonstrates that under shared generation semantics and the chosen synthetic task bank with high oracle coverage, a guarded repair stage cannot be exercised and therefore cannot show measurable benefit. Statistical degeneracy note (artifact‑anchored): the paired contingency is fully concordant (n11=200; n10=n01=n00=0). In this boundary case bootstrap percentile CI collapses to a point mass [0.00,0.00] and exact McNemar returns p=1.00; these values correctly reflect the observed data but are uninformative about potential benefits under alternative designs (independent generation, harder tasks, larger repair budget). Practical guidance (artifact‑grounded): to evaluate verifier‑assisted pipelines, preregister and vary (A) generation semantics (shared vs independent sampling), (B) task difficulty and oracle coverage (avoid ceiling effects), and (C) repair budget/iteration policy (allow repairs to run when failures exist). The full artifact bundle and per‑file hashes permit researchers to (i) re‑run an independent‑generation variant, (ii) increase task difficulty or modify validators, and (iii) explore richer repair policies without reauthoring the original data.
sections.conclusion:
We preregistered and executed an auditable paired emulation study to measure whether verifier‑assistance increases oracle pass rates for LLM→configuration generation. Under the frozen design (shared_initial_candidate semantics, gpt‑5‑mini, deterministic validator, Npairs=200), both baseline and guarded conditions produced oracle‑passing configurations for every pair and repair was never invoked. The observed absolute paired difference is 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.00]; McNemar p=1.00). This null confirmatory outcome is causally traceable to the preregistered generation semantics and high oracle coverage: the guarded repair pathway had no opportunity to act. We release the complete artifact bundle (preregistration, model config, prompts, raw outputs, provider traces, validator traces, execution manifest and SHA‑256 digests) so others can reproduce the accounting and explore independent‑generation or more challenging task/repair settings that can meaningfully test verifier‑assistance. References (representative): [1] Zhou et al., MeshAgent (10.1145/3771567); [2] Wang et al., NetConfEval (10.1145/3656296); [3] Ding, StruSpec (10.31224/7995). Disclosure Statement and exact artifact paths/hashes follow below (mandatory).

References
[1] Y. Zhou et al., "MeshAgent: Enabling Reliable Network Management with Large Language Models," Proc. (2025). DOI: 10.1145/3771567.
[2] C. Wang et al., "NetConfEval: Can LLMs Facilitate Network Configuration?" Proc. (2024). DOI: 10.1145/3656296.
[3] Z. Ding, "Executable but Wrong: Verifier‑Grounded Contracts and Counterexamples for LLM‑Generated Music Programs," 2026. DOI: 10.31224/7995.

This master prompt launched the autonomous post‑lock research run; the Research Director only selected the broad topic family (Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps) and approved the master prompt prior to autonomy lock. All substantive research steps reported here (literature investigation, preregistration, experiment design, code generation, execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, peer review and revision) were performed autonomously after the lock.
- Preregistration (frozen): study id = study-cnd-2026-001; preregistration SHA‑256 = a8969ac01f3b1bb7585872c58a92f72d0752160dd4e6e01cbafbfe0d15073ad2. The preregistration froze primary hypothesis, sampling plan, generation semantics (shared_initial_candidate), model, validator, repair budget (≤1), stopping rules, and analysis executor.
- LLM and adapter: declared model = gpt-5-mini used via hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter; model configuration artifact: execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256 = 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). All provider call traces and raw responses are archived under execution/provider_calls/ and execution/responses/ with per‑file SHA‑256 digests recorded in execution/execution_manifest.json.
- Generation semantics (frozen): shared_initial_candidate (one generated candidate per pair and provided to both baseline and guarded conditions). This preregistered choice produced model_calls_used=200 (one shared generation per 200 pairs) and is the proximate cause the guarded repair stage was never invoked (repair calls invoked = 0). The execution manifest which records these counts and per‑file hashes is archived (execution/execution_manifest.json; see per‑file SHA‑256s inside manifest).
- Validator and oracle: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (deterministic emulation oracle) scored every candidate. Representative scoring artifact: execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json (SHA‑256 = eaf96aec12c30860a6fd70987289cc71104134a3330b99c7e024f244dbd35c1b). All validator traces are archived and hashed.
- Repair policy and budgeting: preregistered maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1; in this run repair calls invoked = 0 (artifact‑backed). Repair prompts would have been archived if used.
- Analysis procedures (frozen): paired_binary_analysis_v1; paired bootstrap 10,000 resamples (seed=1729) and exact McNemar two‑sided test. Confirmatory analysis artifacts: analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (SHA‑256 = 7bc1bd2a42b5ac3f7adb61db47cf8dbe0472f678032abcd1e7c44f92ea2de71c) and analysis/condition_summary.csv (SHA‑256 = 1cb072b4db7c8e29212ef28b97baccb66a507a7c8b8ceaad35b7e84f7976a951).
- Execution and reproducibility: every prompt, model output, provider trace, validator trace, scoring file, manifest and analysis artifact is archived with SHA‑256 digests. Deterministic reconciliation confirms arithmetic and accounting consistency (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json; SHA‑256 = 799b23b993fcc9c04fc4d0a375e975937bc11d9f8c6595d43dce94375411d174).
- Human involvement: pre‑lock collaborative development and approval of the master prompt were performed by the Research Director; no human performed manual substantive editing of the manuscript after the autonomy lock. Pre‑lock development artifacts were not used as empirical evidence unless reproduced under the frozen post‑lock workflow.
- Deviations: none affecting the primary confirmatory analysis; model identifier did not change mid‑run; no pairs excluded; repair stage not triggered. Full execution manifest and per‑file SHA‑256 digests are included in the artifact bundle for audit.
limitations: Confirmatory conclusions are strictly limited to the exact preregistered design (shared_initial_candidate semantics, single declared model gpt‑5‑mini, deterministic_netops_validator_v5, synthetic/emulated task bank of 200).

Shared_initial_candidate execution semantics created a ceiling effect: because the single shared generated candidate per pair passed the deterministic oracle for every task, the guarded repair stage was never exercised (repair calls invoked = 0), preventing any measurable guarded benefit in this run.
Emulation with a deterministic validator and synthetic tasks does not capture full production heterogeneity (real vendor images, runtime nondeterminism, device‑specific quirks).
Single‑model, single‑adapter execution limits external generality across model families and instruction‑tuning variants.
Repair budget was intentionally limited (≤1 call/task) by preregistration; richer iterative repair policies remain unexplored in this run.
Oracle blind spots (uncovered semantic failure modes) remain possible; oracle‑coverage diagnostics are archived and annotated in the artifact bundle.
